props.title: Mata Hari
props.initialSlug: Spy seductress dances between love and betrayal

sections.content: Mata Hari (1931) stands as Greta Garbo's defining femme fatale role, capturing the exotic mystique of WWI's most notorious spy. The film mythologizes the real-life Dutch exotic dancer turned German spy through Hollywood's pre-Code lens, allowing Garbo to push boundaries with provocative dance sequences and seduction scenes that would become impossible after the 1934 Production Code enforcement. Director George Fitzmaurice crafts a lush MGM spectacle that prioritizes glamour over historical accuracy, setting a template for spy films like Dishonored (1931) with Marlene Dietrich and later Mission to Moscow (1943).

sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond its spy narrative into the broader femme fatale archetype that would define film noir. Garbo's portrayal balances sexuality with tragedy, creating a complex character that influenced later films like Notorious (1946) and To Catch a Thief (1955). The real Mata Hari's execution by firing squad in 1917 gives the film its inevitable tragic ending, but Fitzmaurice and Garbo transform historical fact into romantic mythology.

Pre-Code Hollywood's relative freedom allowed Mata Hari to explore themes of sexuality and political intrigue with surprising frankness. The film's exotic dance sequences and bedroom scenes pushed boundaries that would become taboo just three years later. This early sound-era experimentation with mature themes laid groundwork for later spy films like Notorious (1946) and Five Fingers (1952). SUBHEAD: The Evolution of the Female Spy Film

sections.content: Mata Hari established key tropes of the female spy genre that would be revisited and reinvented for decades. The combination of exotic glamour, sexual power, and patriotic betrayal influenced films from Fraulein Doktor (1969) to Red Sparrow (2018). Even modern interpretations like Atomic Blonde (2017) owe a debt to Garbo's pioneering performance.
